title: ROC Curve, AUC and Threshold Selection
abstract:
Classification models predict probabilities, not labels — so somebody has to
choose the threshold that converts one into the other. The ROC curve shows every
possible choice at once by plotting the true positive rate against the false
positive rate as the threshold sweeps, and AUC summarises the whole curve in one
number for comparing models. This document covers both, the geometric rule for
picking a threshold, the probabilistic interpretation of AUC, and the case where
ROC misleads badly and the precision–recall curve should be used instead.

blocks.t: The Problem
From the notes

items:
Used for threshold selection for classification (binary)
 problems.

Classification models like logistic regression don't predict
 $0$ or $1$ — they predict probability values such as $0.45$, $0.39$,
 $0.61$.

We decide a threshold to convert these probabilities to
 predictions, e.g. below $0.5$ is $0$, else $1$.

blocks.t:
The model's raw output is a probability. The label only appears after a threshold
is applied — and that threshold is a choice, not a property of the
model. The ROC curve exists to make the choice visible.
TPR and FPR
From the notes

\boxed{ \text{TPR}=\frac{TP}{TP+FN} }
 \qquad\text{also called recall}

How many actual positives were correctly classified?
The goal is to maximise TPR while selecting the threshold.
\boxed{ \text{FPR}=\frac{FP}{FP+TN} }

How many negative samples are wrongly predicted as positive?
The goal is to minimise FPR while selecting the threshold.
Both denominators are column totals of the confusion matrix

TPR divides by the actual-positive row and FPR by the actual-negative row. Because
each rate uses only one class as its denominator, both are invariant to the
class balance — a property that is ROC's greatest strength and, on severely
imbalanced data, its greatest weakness (\S6).
The Curve

blocks.cap:
Left: the model outputs a distribution of probabilities for each class,
 and a threshold is a vertical cut. Middle: each cut produces one (FPR, TPR)
 pair, and sweeping the threshold traces the ROC curve. Right: the distance from
 each point on the curve to the ideal corner $(0,1)$.

blocks.t: From the notes

The overall goal is to find a threshold which is closest to
$\text{TPR}=1$ and $\text{FPR}=0$. While testing we try different values of the
threshold, like $0.5$, $0.6$, $0.7$, plot them, and choose the one closest to that
point.
Reading the corners

head: Point
Threshold
Behaviour
rows: Predict everything negative. No false alarms, no catches
Predict everything positive. Catches everything, flags everything
Perfect — all positives caught, no negatives flagged

blocks.t:
Lowering the threshold moves you up and to the right: you catch more real
positives (TPR rises) and also flag more negatives (FPR rises). The curve is
therefore always non-decreasing, and it always runs from $(0,0)$ to $(1,1)$.
"Closest to $(0,1)$" is one rule among several

The notes' rule minimises $\sqrt{\text{FPR}^2+(1-\text{TPR})^2}$. Two common
alternatives:

items:
Youden's J: maximise $\text{TPR}-\text{FPR}$ — the vertical
 distance above the diagonal.

Cost-based: minimise $C_{FP}\cdot FP + C_{FN}\cdot FN$, which
 gives the optimal threshold $C_{FP}/(C_{FP}+C_{FN})$ from Topic 09.

blocks.t:
The geometric rules implicitly assume the two errors cost the same. When you know
the costs, use them — they are strictly more informative.
AUC
From the notes
AUC-ROC is used for model comparison, between $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$.

items:
AUC $=1$ is the maximum — the model correctly classifies all
 $+$ and $-$.
AUC $=0$ (or $0.5$) is a poor model.
AUC $=$ Area Under the Curve.

blocks.cap:
Left: four models with increasing separability. Right: AUC is literally
 the shaded area.

blocks.t: What AUC actually means
AUC has an exact probabilistic interpretation:
\boxed{ \text{AUC}=P \left(\text{score}(x^{+}) > \text{score}(x^{-})\right) }

— the probability that a randomly chosen positive is scored higher than
a randomly chosen negative. It is a measure of ranking quality, and it is
identical to the normalised Mann–Whitney U statistic.
Consequences worth knowing:

items:
AUC is threshold-free — it summarises every operating point,
 which is why it is used for model comparison.

It depends only on the ordering of the scores, so any monotone
 rescaling leaves it unchanged. A model can have excellent AUC and badly
 calibrated probabilities.

AUC $=0.5$ is random. AUC $<0.5$ means the model is worse than random —
 and flipping its predictions gives $1-\text{AUC}$, so an AUC of
 $0.2$ is really a good model with reversed labels.

head: AUC
Reading
rows: Worse than random — check your labels

blocks.t: Where ROC Misleads

blocks.cap:
The same model on data with a 0.6% positive rate. ROC-AUC reports
 $0.97$ and looks superb; the precision–recall curve shows precision collapsing
 as soon as recall rises. Both are computed from identical predictions.

blocks.t: The reason: FPR's denominator is enormous

$\text{FPR}=FP/(FP+TN)$. With 19{,}880 negatives and 120 positives, flagging 400
false positives gives $\text{FPR}=400/19{,}880=0.02$ — visually negligible on
the ROC curve. But precision is $120/(120+400)=0.23$: three quarters of the alerts
are wrong, and that is what the investigating team experiences.

The rule: on imbalanced data, report PR-AUC (average precision). Its
baseline is the positive rate rather than a flat $0.5$, so it cannot flatter a
model the way ROC does. Use ROC when the classes are roughly balanced or when you
genuinely care about performance on both classes equally.
Code

import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import (roc_curve, roc_auc_score, auc, confusion_matrix,
                             precision_recall_curve, average_precision_score)
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 4000
X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, 5))
p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(1.8*X[:, 0] + 1.1*X[:, 1] - 0.3)))
y = (rng.random(n) < p).astype(int)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.3,
                                          stratify=y, random_state=0)
model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
scores = model.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]        # PROBABILITIES, not labels

print("raw model output:", scores[:5].round(4))
print("labels only appear after a THRESHOLD is applied")

# =====================================================================
# 1. TPR AND FPR AT EACH THRESHOLD
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'thresh':>7s} {'TP':>5s} {'FP':>5s} {'FN':>5s} {'TN':>5s} "
      f"{'TPR':>7s} {'FPR':>7s}")
for t in [0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.8, 1.0]:
    pred = (scores >= t).astype(int)
    tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(y_te, pred, labels=[0, 1]).ravel()
    tpr = tp / max(tp + fn, 1)                  # = recall
    fpr = fp / max(fp + tn, 1)
    print(f"{t:7.1f} {tp:5d} {fp:5d} {fn:5d} {tn:5d} {tpr:7.4f} {fpr:7.4f}")
# t=0 -> everything positive -> TPR=1, FPR=1  (the point (1,1))
# t=1 -> everything negative -> TPR=0, FPR=0  (the point (0,0))
# Lowering the threshold moves you UP AND RIGHT along the curve.

# =====================================================================
# 2. THE CURVE, AND FINDING THE THRESHOLD CLOSEST TO (0,1)
# =====================================================================
fpr, tpr, thresholds = roc_curve(y_te, scores)
print(f"\nthe curve has {len(thresholds)} points "
      f"(one per distinct score, plus the endpoints)")

dist = np.sqrt(fpr**2 + (1 - tpr)**2)           # distance to the ideal corner
i = int(np.argmin(dist))
print(f"closest to (0,1): threshold {thresholds[i]:.4f}  "
      f"TPR {tpr[i]:.4f}  FPR {fpr[i]:.4f}  distance {dist[i]:.4f}")
print(f"the default 0.5 gives: TPR {tpr[np.argmin(np.abs(thresholds-0.5))]:.4f}  "
      f"FPR {fpr[np.argmin(np.abs(thresholds-0.5))]:.4f}")

# Youden's J -- maximise TPR - FPR
j = int(np.argmax(tpr - fpr))
print(f"Youden's J      : threshold {thresholds[j]:.4f}  "
      f"J = {tpr[j]-fpr[j]:.4f}")

# COST-BASED -- the version to use when you know the costs (Topic 09)
C_FP, C_FN = 1, 20
costs = [( (scores>=t).astype(int) ) for t in thresholds]
tot = [((pr==1)&(y_te==0)).sum()*C_FP + ((pr==0)&(y_te==1)).sum()*C_FN
       for pr in costs]
k = int(np.argmin(tot))
print(f"minimum cost    : threshold {thresholds[k]:.4f}  cost {tot[k]}")
print(f"theory says     : {C_FP/(C_FP+C_FN):.4f}")

# =====================================================================
# 3. AUC -- AND WHAT IT ACTUALLY MEANS
# =====================================================================
print(f"\nAUC via sklearn      : {roc_auc_score(y_te, scores):.6f}")
print(f"AUC as the curve area: {auc(fpr, tpr):.6f}")
print(f"AUC by trapezoid rule: {np.trapezoid(tpr, fpr):.6f}")

# The probabilistic definition, verified by brute force:
pos, neg = scores[y_te == 1], scores[y_te == 0]
pairs = rng.integers(0, len(pos), 200_000), rng.integers(0, len(neg), 200_000)
wins = (pos[pairs[0]] > neg[pairs[1]]).mean() + \
       0.5 * (pos[pairs[0]] == neg[pairs[1]]).mean()
print(f"P(random positive scores above random negative): {wins:.4f}")
# AUC IS that probability -- a measure of RANKING quality.

# It depends only on the ORDER of the scores:
print(f"AUC of scores      : {roc_auc_score(y_te, scores):.6f}")
print(f"AUC of scores^3    : {roc_auc_score(y_te, scores**3):.6f}")
print(f"AUC of log(scores) : {roc_auc_score(y_te, np.log(scores)):.6f}")
# Identical -- any monotone transform preserves AUC. So a model can have
# great AUC and terribly calibrated probabilities.

# AUC < 0.5 means the labels are flipped:
print(f"\nAUC of -scores: {roc_auc_score(y_te, -scores):.4f} "
      f"(= 1 - {roc_auc_score(y_te, scores):.4f})")

# =====================================================================
# 4. MODEL COMPARISON -- what AUC is for
# =====================================================================
models = {
    "logistic":      LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000),
    "random forest": RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, random_state=0),
    "random guess":  None,
}
print(f"\n{'model':16s} {'AUC':>8s}")
for name, m in models.items():
    s = (rng.random(len(y_te)) if m is None
         else m.fit(X_tr, y_tr).predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1])
    print(f"{name:16s} {roc_auc_score(y_te, s):8.4f}")
# Random guessing gives ~0.5 -- the diagonal.

# =====================================================================
# 5. WHERE ROC MISLEADS -- severe imbalance
# =====================================================================
n2 = 30_000
X2 = rng.normal(0, 1, (n2, 5))
p2 = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(2.0*X2[:, 0] + 1.2*X2[:, 1] - 6.5)))
y2 = (rng.random(n2) < p2).astype(int)
X2tr, X2te, y2tr, y2te = train_test_split(X2, y2, test_size=.3,
                                          stratify=y2, random_state=0)
m2 = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(X2tr, y2tr)
s2 = m2.predict_proba(X2te)[:, 1]

print(f"\npositive rate: {y2.mean():.3%}")
print(f"ROC-AUC          : {roc_auc_score(y2te, s2):.4f}   <- looks excellent")
print(f"PR-AUC (avg prec): {average_precision_score(y2te, s2):.4f}")
print(f"PR baseline      : {y2te.mean():.4f}   <- what random would score")

# WHY: FPR's denominator is enormous
f2, t2, th2 = roc_curve(y2te, s2)
i = int(np.argmin(np.abs(t2 - 0.80)))           # at 80% recall
pred = (s2 >= th2[i]).astype(int)
tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(y2te, pred).ravel()
print(f"\nat 80% recall: TP {tp}  FP {fp}  TN {tn}")
print(f"  FPR = {fp}/{fp+tn} = {fp/(fp+tn):.4f}   <- looks tiny on the ROC curve")
print(f"  precision = {tp}/{tp+fp} = {tp/(tp+fp):.4f}   <- what the team feels")
# The same predictions look superb on ROC and poor on PR.

# =====================================================================
# 6. ONE MODEL, MANY OPERATING POINTS
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'goal':<34s} {'threshold':>10s} {'TPR':>7s} {'FPR':>7s}")
targets = [("closest to (0,1)",              None),
           ("recall >= 0.90",                0.90),
           ("recall >= 0.99 (safety)",       0.99),
           ("FPR <= 0.05 (few false alarms)", None)]
i = int(np.argmin(np.sqrt(fpr**2 + (1-tpr)**2)))
print(f"{targets[0][0]:<34s} {thresholds[i]:10.4f} {tpr[i]:7.4f} {fpr[i]:7.4f}")
for label, r in targets[1:3]:
    k = int(np.argmax(tpr >= r))
    print(f"{label:<34s} {thresholds[k]:10.4f} {tpr[k]:7.4f} {fpr[k]:7.4f}")
k = int(np.max(np.flatnonzero(fpr <= 0.05)))
print(f"{targets[3][0]:<34s} {thresholds[k]:10.4f} {tpr[k]:7.4f} {fpr[k]:7.4f}")
# The SAME trained model. Only the threshold changed -- no retraining.
Worked Examples
Building an ROC curve by hand
Four positive samples with scores $[0.9,\,0.8,\,0.6,\,0.4]$ and four negatives $[0.7,\,0.3,\,0.2,\,0.1]$. Predict positive when score $\ge$ threshold $t$.
Area under the curve. Count pairs (positive, negative) where the positive scores higher; ties count half. Out of $4\times4 = 16$ pairs, the positive beats the negative in 14 cases, so
This pair-counting view is exact and equals the trapezoidal area under the ROC points.

Choosing the threshold. The point nearest the ideal corner $(0,1)$ is $(0.25,\,1.00)$ at $t=0.35$ (distance $0.25$). Threshold $0.5$ gives $(0.25,\,0.75)$, distance $0.35$, a more conservative choice. The right choice still depends on the cost of a missed positive versus a false alarm, not just on distance to the corner.
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
ROC is used for threshold selection in binary classification.
 Models like logistic regression predict probabilities, not $0$ or
 $1$, and we decide a threshold to convert them to predictions.

$\text{TPR}=\dfrac{TP}{TP+FN}$ — also called recall: how many
 actual positives were correctly classified. Maximise it.

$\text{FPR}=\dfrac{FP}{FP+TN}$: how many negatives were wrongly predicted
 as positive. Minimise it.

Each threshold gives one $(\text{FPR},\text{TPR})$ point; sweeping the
 threshold traces the curve from $(0,0)$ to $(1,1)$.

The goal is a threshold closest to $\text{TPR}=1$ and
 $\text{FPR}=0$ — the corner $(0,1)$. Alternatives: Youden's J, or the
 cost-based threshold $C_{FP}/(C_{FP}+C_{FN})$.

AUC-ROC is used for model comparison. AUC $=1$ is the
 maximum; $0.5$ is random; below $0.5$ means the labels are
 effectively flipped.

AUC is the probability that a random positive scores above a
 random negative — a measure of ranking, invariant to any monotone
 rescaling. Good AUC does not imply calibrated probabilities.

On imbalanced data ROC flatters the model — FPR's denominator
 is huge. Report PR-AUC instead.
Changing the threshold requires no retraining.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. What does the ROC curve show?

Every possible operating point of a scoring model. Each threshold produces one
(FPR, TPR) pair, and sweeping the threshold from 1 to 0 traces the curve from
$(0,0)$ to $(1,1)$. It separates the model's ranking quality from the
decision you impose on it.
Q. What does an AUC of 0.85 mean?

That a randomly chosen positive receives a higher score than a randomly chosen
negative 85% of the time. It is a ranking measure, equal to the normalised
Mann–Whitney U statistic, and it is invariant to any monotone transform of the
scores.
Q. Your model has AUC 0.97 but is useless in production. How?

Almost certainly severe class imbalance. FPR divides by the huge pool of true
negatives, so thousands of false positives barely register on the ROC curve while
precision collapses. Report PR-AUC, whose baseline is the positive rate rather
than 0.5.
Q. How do you choose the threshold?

Geometrically, the point closest to $(0,1)$, or the one maximising
$\text{TPR}-\text{FPR}$. Better, when you know the costs: minimise
$C_{FP}\cdot FP+C_{FN}\cdot FN$, giving $t^*=C_{FP}/(C_{FP}+C_{FN})$. Best of
all, let the business constraint decide — "catch 90% of fraud" or "the team
can handle 5{,}000 alerts".
Q. Do you retrain to change the threshold?

No. The model outputs probabilities; the threshold is applied afterwards. This is
the practical payoff of a probabilistic output over the perceptron's hard label
(Topic 44).
Q. An AUC of 0.2 — what happened?

The model ranks negatives above positives, which almost always means the labels or
the predicted class column are inverted. Flipping the scores gives AUC $=0.8$, so
there is a good model hiding behind a sign error.
Q. Can a model have high AUC but poor probability calibration?

Yes, and it is common. AUC depends only on the ordering of the scores, so a model
that ranks perfectly but outputs $0.6$ for everything positive and $0.4$ for
everything negative has AUC $=1.0$ and useless probabilities. Check calibration
separately with a reliability curve or Brier score.
